content.text: A map (or dictionary) is a data structure used to store key-value pairs. It allows for efficient lookups, insertions, and deletions of values based on their associated keys. Maps are essential for fast, direct access to data and are widely used in applications such as database indexing, network routing, and web programming.

items: Stores pairs: A map stores pairs of keys and values, where each key is unique.
Efficient operations: Operations like inserting, retrieving, or deleting values are efficient, often O(1) for many map types.
No duplicates: Maps do not allow duplicate keys, but values can be duplicated.
Put: O(1) for most maps (except TreeMap, which is O(log n)).
Get: O(1) for most maps (except TreeMap, which is O(log n)).
Remove: O(1) for most maps (except TreeMap, which is O(log n)).
Iteration: O(n), where n is the number of entries in the map.

content.text: A HashMap uses a hash function to map keys to indices in an internal array, which allows for fast retrieval of values based on their associated keys.

items: Unordered storage: HashMap does not maintain any order of the keys.
Null keys: HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values.
Thread safety: HashMap is not thread-safe. If used in a multi-threaded environment, consider using ConcurrentHashMap or manually synchronizing access.
Performance:
Put:  O(1) on average, because it hashes the key and inserts it into the appropriate index.
Get: O(1) on average, because the key is hashed, and the corresponding value is retrieved in constant time.
Remove: O(1) on average.
Iteration: O(n), as we need to traverse all entries in the map.

content.text: A Hashtable is a legacy map implementation that also uses a hash function for mapping keys to values. It is very similar to HashMap, but it has some important differences in behavior and features.

items: Thread safety: Unlike HashMap, Hashtable is synchronized and thread-safe, which makes it suitable for concurrent environments.
Null keys/values: Hashtable does not allow null keys or null values, unlike HashMap, which allows one null key and multiple null values.
Performance:
Put: O(1) on average.
Get: O(1) on average.
Remove: O(1) on average.
Iteration: O(n), where n is the number of entries.
Thread Safety: Hashtable is synchronized, making it thread-safe, while HashMap is not.
Null Keys and Values: HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values, whereas Hashtable does not allow null keys or values.
Legacy: Hashtable is part of the legacy collection classes, while HashMap is part of the modern Java collections framework.

content.text: A LinkedHashMap maintains a doubly-linked list of the entries in the map, preserving the order in which they were inserted, while still providing fast lookups.

items: Order: It maintains the insertion order of keys.
Null keys: Allows one null key and multiple null values.
Thread safety: Not thread-safe.
Performance:
Put: O(1) on average.
Get: O(1) on average.
Remove: O(1) on average.
Iteration: O(n), where n is the number of entries in the map.

content.text: A TreeMap is a map that stores keys in sorted order using a red-black tree.

items: Order: It maintains keys in ascending order (or according to a comparator if provided).
Null keys: Does not allow null keys, but allows null values.
Thread safety: Not thread-safe.
Performance:
Put: O(log n), as the red-black tree needs to maintain balance.
Get: O(log n).
Remove: O(log n).
Iteration: O(n), where n is the number of entries in the map, as it involves traversing the tree in sorted order.

content.text: The Map interface in Java defines methods for associating keys with values, including:

items: put(K key, V value): Inserts a key-value pair into the map.
get(Object key): Retrieves the value associated with the key.
remove(Object key): Removes the key-value pair.
containsKey(Object key): Checks if a key exists in the map.
containsValue(Object value): Checks if a value exists in the map.
size(): Returns the number of key-value pairs in the map.
clear(): Removes all key-value pairs.

content.text: Maps are essential data structures for efficiently storing key-value pairs. The choice of map implementation depends on the use case:

items: HashMap: Best for unordered, fast lookups with average O(1) performance.
Hashtable: Thread-safe version of HashMap, but with slight performance overhead and does not allow null keys.
LinkedHashMap: Maintains insertion order, with O(1) performance for basic operations.
TreeMap: Best for sorted key storage with O(log n) performance, ideal for range queries and key navigation.

content.text: Each implementation provides unique benefits suited to different types of applications, making maps highly versatile.
